questions.q: Why does this lesson say feedback like "that was pretty good" or "you seemed nervous" doesn't actually help a candidate improve?
options: Because it doesn't name a specific moment or category, so it gives the candidate nothing concrete to actually change next time
Because it is factually incorrect in every case
Because panels are not allowed to use informal language
Because only written feedback is considered valid
questions.explain: Useful feedback ties a specific moment to a specific category and ideally shows what a stronger version would look like — vague impressions don't give the candidate anything actionable.

questions.q: What does the "Breadth" rubric category evaluate?
options: Whether the candidate spoke loudly enough to be heard
Whether the candidate used a whiteboard during the session
Whether the presentation covered the architecture domains the scenario actually touches, rather than quietly skipping one
Whether the panel agreed with every decision made
questions.explain: Breadth specifically checks domain coverage — for example, whether a Carrow Equipment presentation addressed sharing, integration, identity, and application architecture rather than focusing on just one.

questions.q: According to this lesson, what does the "Defensibility" category actually test, as distinct from whether the panel agreed with a choice?
options: Whether every decision was approved unanimously by the panel
Whether each major decision had a stated reason the candidate could explain under direct questioning, including a rejected alternative where relevant
Whether the candidate used the most expensive Salesforce product available
Whether the candidate avoided all forms of criticism during Q&A
questions.explain: Defensibility is about whether a reason exists and can be explained, not about whether the panel happens to like the specific choice made.

questions.q: What does this lesson recommend a candidate do when receiving critical feedback, instead of immediately explaining or justifying the choice being criticized?
options: Argue down every piece of critical feedback in the moment to defend the original decision
Ignore all feedback that doesn't come from an official instructor
Immediately redesign the entire solution on the spot during the feedback session
Hear the observation fully, take notes, ask a clarifying question if needed, and reflect afterward on which feedback to act on
questions.explain: Arguing down feedback in the moment typically means absorbing less of it — the recommended approach is hearing it fully first, then deciding afterward what to act on.

questions.q: Why does this lesson say giving rubric-based feedback to a peer also benefits the person giving it, not just the person receiving it?
options: Because giving feedback earns extra credit toward course completion
Because the person giving feedback is exempt from ever being evaluated themselves
Because noticing a specific weakness (like a disconnected walkthrough) in someone else's session sharpens the reviewer's own eye for the same pattern in their own future presentations
Because feedback sessions are scored by the panel as a separate exercise
questions.explain: Peer review is framed as a two-way skill-building exercise — reviewing against the rubric trains the reviewer to catch the same issues in their own work later.
